name: Lena Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We rent 280 acres from the church estate at Kelby, so I'm a tenant farmer, which means I farm land I'll never own. It's 500 ewes, about 90 acres of wheat, and a strip of vegetables for the growers' co-op box scheme. In lambing I'm out every three hours through the night with a head torch; the rest of the year it's checking feet, moving flocks, and the endless forms for the estate and the grants. I love the ewes, honestly, even the stupid ones.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, how do the sums work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Badly, most months. My husband Sami works with me three days and drives a parcel van the other two, because the farm alone doesn't cover the mortgage on our bungalow in the village. The rent review on the farm is next autumn and the estate's agent has already hinted it's going up. We've got about three weeks of bills put by, if nothing breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the AI does my forms a bit faster and that's it. I'll take that, to be fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful for the paperwork and not much else, which is what I've found already. I used a chatbot once to tidy up a grant application and it was fine. At the co-op meeting I'd say the real fight is still the supermarket price for lamb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the rent review and lamb prices still decide whether we stay. The AI isn't my problem; a landlord with a spreadsheet is. If the rent goes up by a fifth, we're in real trouble even in the calmest world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the chatbot for the grant forms, maybe once a month. I'd get the co-op to make a joint case to the estate before the rent review, so it's eight tenants talking, not just me. And I'd sell the 30 oldest ewes this autumn instead of keeping them one more year, for the cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, the usual kind of worried. Nothing here takes it away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the rent does go up, what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The vegetable strip goes first, because it's the most hours for the least money. Then Sami would ask the parcel firm for a fourth day. I'd hate that, because he's the one who notices a lame ewe before I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible for the squeeze?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarkets, and the estate to a lesser degree. The church owns the land and talks about community on Sundays, and then puts the rent up on families who've farmed it for twenty years. I'd say that politely to the agent, and less politely to Sami.

say: I'd say AI helps with **paperwork** and not much else, from my own experience.
I'd tell the co-op the real fight is the **supermarket price** for lamb.
think: I think the **rent review** and lamb prices decide whether we stay, not AI.
A **rise of a fifth** in the rent would put us in real trouble.
do: Keep using the **chatbot** for grant forms about once a month.
Get the co-op's **eight tenants** to make a joint case before the rent review.
Sell the **30 oldest ewes** this autumn for cash.
feel: **Worried** in the usual way, because nothing in this picture eases the **rent**.
S0.quote: The AI isn't my problem; a landlord with a spreadsheet is.
fieldNote: Lena's pressure is **tenancy**: a rent review next autumn and three weeks of savings.
She already uses **AI lightly** for grant forms and sees it as a small help.
Her instinct is **collective**: eight tenants talking together, not one.
Her husband's **second job** is the household's buffer, and she worries about losing his eye on the flock.

steps.text: Get the eight estate tenants to make a joint case on rent
Keep using a chatbot for grant forms once a month
Sell the 30 oldest ewes this autumn for cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, checking, booking. That's the forms and the grant schemes. That bit of my week could shrink, and I wouldn't cry about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good if it gives farmers back their evenings, and bad if it lets the estate and the buyers squeeze us faster. I'd post that the gains need to stay on the farm. And I'd say the co-op should buy the tools together so small farms aren't left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it helps me a little and helps the big operators a lot. They'll plan with it, sell with it and buy with it better than I can. The robots coming slowly is fine for my ewes, but the price gap with the big farms grows every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a couple of the other tenants have tried it, I'd use one of the farm-planning apps for the flock records and the grant forms. I'd suggest the co-op shares a subscription, maybe forty pounds a month split eight ways. And I'd look at taking on shearing work for neighbours in June, because a good shearer is still a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. A bit hopeful about the paperwork, a bit sick about the prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for the other tenants. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can't afford to pay for something that doesn't work. Gareth at Low Farm always tries everything first, he's got a bit more money behind him. When he says it's good, I'll do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the shearing actually bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two pounds a sheep, so maybe two thousand pounds in total. I can do 150 sheep on a good day, and three weeks of shearing in June is the whole savings account twice over. My back would complain, but my back always complains.

I'd post that the co-op should buy **tools together** so small farms keep up.
think: I think it helps me a little and helps the **big operators** a lot.
The **price gap** with big farms would grow every year.
do: Start a **farm-planning app** for flock records once other tenants have tried it.
Propose the co-op splits a **forty-pound subscription** eight ways.
Take on **shearing work** for neighbours in June for extra income.
feel: **Mixed**: hopeful about the paperwork, **sick** about the prices.
S1.quote: I can do 150 sheep on a good day, and three weeks of shearing in June is the whole savings account twice over.
fieldNote: Lena is **steady**: she waits for a neighbour with more money to test the tools first.
She sees the real risk as **price pressure** from big farms using AI better.
Her side plan is **physical**: shearing at two pounds a head.
She's hopeful about **paperwork** relief but not about her income.

steps.text: Start a farm-planning app for flock records once Gareth has tested it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2031. Lambing robots, I suppose. I can't picture it, but I couldn't picture a smartphone once either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs public money now, not later: support for small farms and a guaranteed price for food. I'd write to our MP and say it at the co-op. I'd also say that land shouldn't go to whoever has the most robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the estate would rent the farm to a big robot operator the moment one offers more. From 2028 the forms, the planning and the selling are all done by AI, so the big farms get cheaper fast. By 2031 or so, a tenant like me is the most expensive thing on the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI properly from the start, because I'd have no choice, and push the co-op to do the selling and buying together through it. I'd ask the estate for a longer tenancy right away, ten years, before anyone else can bid. And I'd talk to Sami about him going full-time at the parcel firm while that work still exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if I'm honest. The kind of frightened where you start being very practical so you don't cry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between AGI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're the years I'd fight for the tenancy. While the robots aren't ready, the ewes still need me, and I'm good with them, the best lamber in the valley. After that, it's down to who the estate prefers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noor and Idris?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Noor and my son Idris that the farm might not be ours to keep, and that's not their fault or ours. Noor would ask straight away about the dog. Children ask about the dog.

say: I'd call for **public money** now: support for small farms and a **guaranteed price**.
I'd say land shouldn't go to whoever owns the **most robots**.
think: I think the estate rents to a **big robot operator** as soon as one bids more.
By 2031 a tenant like me is the **most expensive thing** on the land.
do: Ask the estate for a **ten-year tenancy** straight away, before others bid.
Push the co-op to **sell and buy together** using AI from the start.
Talk with Sami about going **full-time** at the parcel firm.
feel: **Frightened**, and turning very **practical** to keep from crying.
S2.quote: By 2031 or so, a tenant like me is the most expensive thing on the land.
fieldNote: Lena expects to **lose the tenancy**, the core of the household income, within about five years.
She would adopt AI **because she must**, a shift from her usual wait-and-see.
The **three-year gap** is when she'd fight for a long lease while her skills still count.
Her story about the kids and **the dog** shows the fear under the practical voice.

steps.text: Write to the MP for small-farm support and a guaranteed food price
Run the flock and grant forms through AI tools from 2028
Push the co-op to sell lamb and buy feed together
Talk with Sami about him going full-time at the parcel firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Long enough to plan, short enough to feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set the rules, so let's set them: tenant protections, help for small farms, and land kept for families. I'd say it at the co-op AGM and online. I'd be one of the loud ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I can maybe make myself the person the estate can't easily replace. If I'm the one who knows the land, runs the AI well and keeps the flock healthy, that's worth something. I'm not sure it's worth enough, but it's a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a short course on the farm software through the co-op, maybe a winter evening class in town. I'd try for a ten-year tenancy at the rent review next autumn. And I'd build up the shearing and the veg boxes as a second leg, so we're not standing on the farm alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. Five years is enough to try things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes on your farm between AGI in 2031 and robots in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office side goes first. A third of my week is grants, records, ordering feed and selling lambs, and the AI takes that first. Then the hands-on side, the lambing and the feet and the moving, is still mine until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said the co-op a lot. What if the co-op splits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's every tenant for themselves, and the big ones win. I've seen it happen at the machinery ring, people fell out over who got the baler first. I'd rather keep it together, even with Gareth being annoying.

say: I'd say five years is time to set **tenant protections** and help small farms.
I'd be one of the **loud ones** at the co-op AGM and online.
think: I think I can make myself **hard to replace** if I run the AI and the flock well.
I'm not sure that's **worth enough** to keep the tenancy.
do: Take a **winter evening course** on farm software through the co-op.
Push for a **ten-year tenancy** at next autumn's rent review.
Grow the **shearing and veg boxes** into a second income.
feel: **Anxious**, but in a way she can **work with**, because five years allows trying.
S3.quote: A third of my week is grants, records, ordering feed and selling lambs, and the AI takes that first.
fieldNote: Five years moves Lena from alarm to **anxious with a plan**: courses, a long lease, a second income.
She clearly splits her week into **thinking work** and hands-on work and sees which goes first.
Her faith is in the **co-op holding together**, and she knows how fragile that is.

steps.text: Take a winter evening course on farm software through the co-op
Push for a ten-year tenancy at next autumn's rent review
Grow shearing and veg boxes into a second income
Speak at the co-op AGM for tenant protections

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Noor would be twenty-three. That changes how it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to plan land reform and support for farm families, and nobody gets to waste it. I'd want the co-op to own its own machines and robots when they come. That would be my message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel there's room to breathe. The kids would be grown, and if the co-op owns the robots, maybe I become the one who runs the flock with them. I still don't trust the estate, but ten years is long enough to find other land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start small: one AI tool a year, once others have tried it. I'd push the co-op to start a fund to buy shared machines, maybe twenty pounds a month from each family. And I'd keep the shearing going and help Noor work out what to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a knot in my stomach about the rent, but a smaller knot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help Noor decide what to study. What would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Noor to study something with people in it, like teaching or medicine, and keep a bit of land in her heart. She loves the lambs. I'd hate for her to think farming is only for robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent, always the rent. AI or no AI, the estate's agent can put the rent up. Three weeks of savings doesn't change in ten years unless something else changes.

I'd want the co-op to **own its own robots** when they come.
think: I think there's **room to breathe**, because the kids would be grown.
Ten years is long enough to **find other land** if the estate turns.

Start a **co-op machine fund** at twenty pounds a month per family.
Keep the **shearing** going for extra income.

S4.quote: AI or no AI, the estate's agent can put the rent up.
fieldNote: The decade lets Lena picture a future where the **co-op owns the robots** and she runs the flock.
Her mood stays **anxious** because the rent and **thin savings** don't change with time.
She'd want her daughter to keep **land in her heart** while studying something else.

steps.text: Add one tried-and-tested AI tool to the farm each year
Start a co-op machine fund at twenty pounds a month per family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to fight for the tenancy before the big operators come knocking. What would help is a law that gives tenant farmers first refusal and long leases, and public money for co-ops to buy shared robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land itself. Everyone asks about jobs, but whoever owns the land owns the future, robots or not. I'd want people to remember that tenants have no say.

headlineQuote: Whoever owns the land owns the future, robots or not.
portrait: Lena is a **tenant farmer** with 500 ewes and wheat on church estate land.
Her household runs on **three weeks** of savings and her husband's **parcel van** job.
She blames **supermarkets** and landlords, and puts her trust in the **co-op**.
She uses AI **now and then** and would adopt it fully if forced, after neighbours test it.
Her mood runs **anxious** to alarmed, driven by fear of losing the **tenancy**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there's no time to secure the **tenancy**.
whatWouldHelp: A law giving tenants **first refusal** and long leases, plus **public money** for co-op robots.
